chapters.subtitle: the life of a woman who managed to keep painting

stops.title: Her story
stops.caption: ON MY WAY HOME TO MOTHER, I STOPPED IN CHICAGO WHERE MY COUSIN SIMON TOOK THIS PICTURE

quote.text: So, now you're getting a picture book, an autobiography, some travel notes, a touch of homely philosophy and if it all works out maybe a recipe or two (but no ARTSPEAK).
quote.label: From the opening pages of her book

stops.moreLabel: A first look at her work

quote.text: So I have managed to fit my work in the spaces between my husband, children and housekeeping, and I still feel “avant garde” when I leave the bed unmade. As a woman painter who married, raised children, and kept the house (with all that it entails), I have found the most precious work-necessity to be continuity, and like most precious things, it is rare.
quote.label: From her artist statement

quote.text: Oh yes, I also carry a pocket-size dime store notebook for daily travel notes.
quote.label: From her book: TRAVEL

quote.text: This was the first divorce in the family and considered so shameful that his name was never mentioned, he was cut out of group pictures, and it wasn't until after my mother died that I found this picture, after having seen this one all my life.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: Her mother divorced her father, William Ammerman, when Leah was an infant.

quote.text: At the Steiners, my cousins Mel and Simon and I used to draw pictures on a shared easel-slate. The boys would draw cars, boats and cowboys, and I would draw pretty ladies with curly hair.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: After the divorce her mother moved to Chicago.

quote.text: Mother was handy at everything. She taught me how to sew, to make electrical repairs, and to be intolerant of shoddiness.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: Between the ages of six and ten she went to seven different schools.

stops.caption: SHOWING OFF ON "MAX"

quote.text: I drew a lot of horses during the farm years, some from life and some copied from farm journals. I also painted some landscapes on cardboard with cheap poster paint.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: The family moved to “Sunrise Farm,” a collective farm near Saginaw, Michigan.

quote.text: When I was sixteen I received an anonymous gift, a complete set of oil paints, brushes, linseed oil, turpentine and palette in a beautiful wooden box (I still have the box).
quote.label: From her book: OLD STUFF

stops.title: Art school in New York
stops.caption: MY FIRST ART SCHOOL PAINTING (just like the teacher's)

quote.text: We plunged directly into oil painting, no fooling around with learning how to draw, perspective, color, painting techniques... just paint like the teacher. So I did.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: After high school she went to art school in New York City.

stops.caption: ME, SAM (learning to knit), AND CHARLOTTE IN OUR "BOHEMIAN" LIVING-ROOM-STUDIO

quote.text: He also gave me a panel of beautiful paper glued to masonite that I was afraid to "ruin." It was dauntingly elegant. When he found out that I hadn't painted anything on it, he guessed why and took a brush loaded with watercolor, smeared it over the board and said, "There, now go ahead and paint something!"
quote.label: From her book: OLD STUFF

fact.text: The artists Ben and Bernarda Shahn lived nearby and encouraged young artists.

quote.text: Nine months later our son Daniel was born in a blacked out hospital in Monmouth, New Jersey during an air raid alert.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: During the war she and Lee Drasin were married secretly in Alexandria, Virginia.

stops.title: Beetles
stops.subtitle: the accidental watercolorist
stops.caption: ONE OF THE MANY BEETLE PAINTINGS I DID IN THE PROCESS OF TEACHING MYSELF WATERCOLOR TECHNIQUE

quote.text: One fine day, while browsing the shelves of the Marin County Library, I found a large volume of color photographs of beetles from all over the world. I was so taken with their color and bizarre forms that I went right out and bought watercolors, brushes and paper and tried to paint them.
quote.label: From her autobiography

quote.text: I've tried to make my students (many of them exhibiting artists in other media) aware of the ordinary things around them. … It's a great pleasure to see an artist take to watercolor and develop a personal style. It doesn't happen often, but when it does I feel like a mother with a gifted child.
quote.label: From her autobiography

chapters.title: Mill Valley
chapters.subtitle: roots, more roots and FINALLY ROOTED

quote.text: …a tall, dark, handsome young man who said he was on his way to Mexico to explore caves for blind fish. (The rest of the year he was a Harvard medical student.) I had never heard of blind fish so I fell in love.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: Leah and Herman Schwartz were married in Boston on November 1, 1952.

stops.title: Peter and David
stops.caption: WITH MY HANDS FULL (literally and figuratively) OF PETER AND DAVY

quote.text: In desperation, I sculpted a clay head of Davy before he learned how to climb out of his play pen. I worked on it at the kitchen sink while Peter napped.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: Peter was born in January 1954 and David in February 1955.

quote.text: After a few years, we bought a waterfront lot across the street and I then designed, and we had built, a white clapboard, three-story house with a vaguely New England look.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: In 1954 the family moved to California and found a house in Mill Valley.

stops.title: Time to paint
stops.subtitle: if everything else is taken care of
stops.caption: Hilaritas House, 1958-59

quote.text: When the children started going to school full time I began painting full time, 9:30 to 3, five days a week, unless the kids had to be taken to doctor, dentist, orthodontist, orthopedist (broken bones), Little League, swimming lessons... the whole goddamned middle class suburban trip.
quote.label: From her autobiography

fact.text: She had her first one-man show in San Francisco in the sixties.

quote.text: I paint in my studio in Mill Valley during the week and do slave labor in Bolinas on weekends. … We may be nuts, but we love to work, and making things is a great pleasure to both of us.
quote.label: From the opening pages of her book

fact.text: Herman kept a world-famous collection of succulent plants in a greenhouse in Bolinas.

stops.title: Her house designs
stops.caption: 1,650 sq. ft. house for small waterfront lot

quote.text: I have a secret yearning to be an architect and I designed the house we live in, converted our Bolinas barn-shack to a farm house, and was delighted to be asked to design a house for my young friend Lisa Adler who lives in the Sierras.
quote.label: From her book: INTERIORS

quote.text: These paintings were done during the unsettled years of my life. Until I was almost forty, I didn't have the kind of stability or free time necessary for producing a consistent body of work.
quote.label: From her book: OLD STUFF

quote.text: In the early sixties I had a brief fling with flinging. I smeared, spattered and poured paint onto canvases spread on the floor. … It was fun for awhile, but I don't think abstractly and I don't worship paint for its own sake so I resumed painting what I truly love: the real, funny, beautiful, ironic visual world.
quote.label: From her book: ABSTRACT

quote.text: In the sixties and seventies, when the U.S was in a ferment of civil rights demonstrations and Vietnam war protests, I expressed my concern in painting, multimedia constructions, and collages which were seen by thousands of people at the huge Sausalito Arts Festival.
quote.label: From her book: SOCIAL COMMENT

quote.text: I create scenarios, in my mind, of the lives of the people involved with these places. Every detail is part of the fabric of someone's life, so I spend a lot of time getting the details right. A crumpled bit of trash has to look authentic; it adds to the feeling of time and place.
quote.label: From her book: ON THE ROAD

quote.text: I used to paint landscapes from my old Ford Econoline van that had an engine housing between the front seats. The top of the housing was flat and formed a convenient table for paints, and the steering wheel was at a good angle for watercolor painting. In my portable studio I could even paint in the rain.
quote.label: From her book: LANDSCAPE

quote.text: I love these glimpses of people on the street, walking their dogs, waiting for buses, standing on street corners waiting for the light to change. I'm also interested in "street furniture": bus shelters, mailboxes, poles, posts, mysterious black boxes, hydrants, curbs, manhole covers - things we all see but rarely notice.
quote.label: From her book: STREET SCENES

quote.text: I've been working on a series of watercolors of a bunch of spring flowers (with self-portrait in the background). At first the flowers are fresh and bright and I am dim and dull ...but as the flowers fade I look better and better ...Ha Ha, they fade faster than I do!
quote.label: From a letter to Judy Adler, in her book: PORTRAITS

quote.text: In recent years I've done a lot of still lifes, mostly fruits and vegetables. Patient, colorful and varied in shape, they make ideal models, they last longer than flowers, and they never get restless.
quote.label: From her book: STILL LIFE

stops.title: Interiors
stops.subtitle: gimme shelter
stops.caption: Bolinas, Bathroom, Bedroom, And View To The Sea

quote.text: From my mother I inherited a love of houses (God knows we lived in a great number and variety of dwellings). … Most people don't give a damn about southern exposures, covered entries, convenient kitchens, "traffic flow," closet space, where the sun rises in the winter time, or whether a room has enough corners. I do.
quote.label: From her book: INTERIORS

stops.title: Flowers
stops.subtitle: in love with bloom
stops.caption: White Iris With San Francisco Skyline

quote.text: Most of my flower watercolors were painted from my husband's dazzling flower garden on the edge of the bay with the San Francisco skyline for a backdrop (which I have used in several paintings).
quote.label: From her book: FLOWERS

quote.text: It is a miracle of white granite boulders, spring flowers, crystal lakes, cascading streams and occasionally a grassy, flower-spangled meadow. … We hike all day and read to each other by kerosene lamp at night.
quote.label: From her book: HIGH SIERRA

quote.text: I used to be so petrified at the thought of flying that all I could manage was to go on every other overseas trip with my travel-obsessed husband.
quote.label: From her book: TRAVEL

quote.text: The next day HH&M went off to Siena for the day and I had Gello to myself (except for the Padre, who didn't surface, and a herd of black goats that did). I took this opportunity to paint a watercolor of the kitchen and cook some onions, peppers and tomatoes (from the farmer down the road) for a pasta sauce.
quote.label: From her book: TRAVEL

fact.text: In September 1974 she and Herman drove to Italy with their friends Herb and Maggie Rosen.

quote.text: I gave a painting demonstration every morning, we painted on location all day, and had an exhibition and critique with our Metaxa in the evening before going out to dinner. After a bit of Metaxa, everything looked just dandy.
quote.label: From her book: TRAVEL

fact.text: Her friend Linda Pearman asked her to lead a painting workshop; they chose the Greek island of Naxos.

quote.text: The next morning I went out at 6a.m., sat on a curbstone and painted a street scene until stiff with cold.
quote.label: From her book: TRAVEL

fact.text: In May 1983 she travelled to Japan with a group of friends.

quote.text: I once sat on a fallen Stonehenge rock and painted, using the fresh rain water in a hollow of the rock. The painting is dismal, dreary and drab.
quote.label: From her book: TRAVEL

stops.moreLabel: Britain, the desert, and her other notebook

stops.title: Watercolor
stops.caption: Six Days On The Petaluma River

quote.text: The trick with watercolor is to let the color flow but not to let it get away from you. The battle between letting go and control is the basic way of watercolor.
quote.label: From her autobiography

quote.text: I love the process of what I do. I enjoy the feel of a brush on canvas, the smell of turpentine, the flow of color on a fresh sheet of watercolor paper, and the intense pleasure of making things (it must be genetic).
quote.label: From her autobiography

stops.title: Things to look at
stops.caption: Tin of found objects

quote.text: This compulsion is not a need to create ART but a need to preserve ephemeral things that I love to look at, a need to "give out" some of what I take in. The things I love to look at might be anything: newspaper clippings, flowers, pieces of junk or local landscapes.
quote.label: From her autobiography

stops.moreLabel: Her collections, and junk turned into art

stops.title: Her travel kit
stops.caption: Jars of sand from her travels

quote.text: I travel light, with one carry-on bag and a small backpack with camera and painting gear, small plastic paintbox, 2 good watercolor brushes, sketch book, small water bottle, and a chocolate bar, all fitted into a quilted tea-cozy which makes a good cushion.
quote.label: From her book: TRAVEL

stops.moreLabel: Small sketches made on the road

stops.title: The book, 1990
stops.caption: Front Jacket: SPRING THICKET, 11"x15", 1981

quote.text: The first idea for this book was for a small "tasteful" volume of travel sketches with excerpts from my travel notebooks. Little by little, through the process of "Oh, you can't leave that out," and "I really would like to include —," this book has developed into the story of the life of a woman who managed to keep painting.
quote.label: From the opening pages of her book

fact.text: The book was published in 1990 by Strawberry Press in Mill Valley.
